page.title: Audit trail
page.subtitle: Every recorded action by your agency, newest first — who did it, when, and what changed. Actions that were <r>refused</r> are recorded too, and marked as such: an attempt someone's role did not allow is often the line that matters most. Append-only and hash-chained, so alteration is detectable. Other agencies' actions are never shown.
page.errorFallback: could not load the audit trail

chainVerified.title: ✓ Chain verified — every entry links to the one before it.
chainVerified.body: Each record is hashed together with its predecessor, so editing or removing any entry breaks every hash after it. Re-checked just now.
chainVerified.caveat: What this does not prove: that every action was recorded in the first place. The chain shows nothing here was altered or removed — an entry that was never written leaves no trace to break. Those write failures are counted and alerted on separately, so a missing record is caught by monitoring rather than by this check.

chainFailed.title: ✗ Chain verification FAILED
chainFailed.body: The log has been altered since it was written, or entries are missing. Everything from that point on should be treated as unreliable and investigated — do not rely on this trail as evidence until it is explained.

page.title: How ITTU works — a quick guide
page.subtitle: ITTU (Infiltrate, Trace, Takedown & Uncover) turns financial-crime response from reactive to proactive. Four modules chain into one investigation: hunt intel from scammers, trace the money across bank and crypto rails, score the wallet network, and generate the legal action — every step preserved for court.
page.flowBody: It all hangs off a <caseLink>Case File</caseLink>. You start at its <intake>Intake</intake> stage — log a victim report or run a honeypot — then the stage tracker walks the case through the four modules. A scammer chat (or a report) surfaces a wallet and a mule account; that wallet feeds the bridge (fiat ↔ crypto) and the graph (risk scoring); the scored targets feed Uncover, which emits the freeze request and agency notifications. Everything is custody-hashed from the first message to the final document.
page.postureIntro: Every external boundary (the honeypot LLM, blockchain data, bank feeds, notifications) sits behind an adapter that runs in one of two modes. The badge in the top bar shows the current mode.

poc.body: The safe default — fully offline, deterministic, no credentials. Scripted honeypot replays, blockchain fixtures, synthetic bank data. PDFs and custody hashing are real; notifications go to a mock sink (nothing leaves the system).

live.body: The same code against real sources — a real LLM, the Tronscan API, bank feeds, agency webhooks. Requires explicit config and keys, and fails loudly if they are missing rather than silently degrading.

page.scenariosIntro: The honeypot ships three MVP scam typologies. Start one from the <honeypotLink>Honeypot</honeypotLink> screen; each replays a full conversation whose disclosed entities are validated into court-usable intel.
page.riskModelBody: TAKEDOWN scores each wallet with an unsupervised Isolation Forest over 12 behavioral features, backed by 5 deterministic typology detectors — peeling chain, rapid relay, circular (wash), structuring, and fan-out. The model is validated against the Elliptic Data Set (203k Bitcoin transactions) for ROC-AUC / precision / recall.

page.footerTip: Tip: the fastest way to see the full chain is to start a honeypot session, then take the disclosed wallet into the Takedown graph.
